text.title: Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor
text.purpose: Burak and Fiete model a group of interacting neurons that retains a continuous value after an input ends. This chapter follows spikes through their effects at synapses and back into firing, then derives how random spike timing displaces the stored value.

text.title: Recurrent spikes renew decaying synaptic activity
text.summary: **Neural mechanism.** How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than the duration of a spike? In this model, each spike leaves a synaptic activation that decays gradually. Incoming activations determine new firing rates; the resulting spikes renew those activations. This feedback can support activity after the external stimulus has ended.

extra_reader_text_inventory.checked: How can brief spikes sustain a state and introduce noise into it? The Gaussian approximation concerns summed inputs in a large population, not the exact spike train of each cell.

text.title: The network's return flow determines the lasting memory change
text.summary: **Neural mechanism.** A spike perturbs many aspects of a network's state. Most of those changes decay as the state returns to the attractor. To calculate memory loss, we need the one change that survives: the displacement to a different fixed point. We assume a smooth continuous family with one neutral memory direction, while all other local modes decay. The disturbance must be small enough that the first order response describes the return flow.

extra_reader_text_inventory.checked: Find the coordinate shift remaining after all locally stable modes decay. Small disturbances and decay of other modes are needed; changing one weight does not determine the eigenstructure.

text.title: Projecting spike fluctuations gives the diffusion coefficient
text.summary: **Neural mechanism.** We can now calculate how much random displacement remains after the stable components have relaxed. Each cell's random spikes disturb its outgoing synaptic activation; the circuit's return flow determines the lasting shift in memory. This calculation uses the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions, with rates and return flow evaluated near one fixed point.

extra_reader_text_inventory.checked: Calculate variance of the retained coordinate increment. The window must be longer than stable relaxation and short enough for coefficients to stay local.

Symmetric connections make each cell affect another cell's input with the same weight that it receives in return, while their firing responses can still differ. We retain the common synaptic time constant, a stable continuous family, and the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions.

text.title: Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays
text.purpose: In the memory-network model, random changes in a stored angle accumulate over time. This chapter extends the local spreading calculation to longer delays, where boundaries, angular wraparound, and systematic drift can change the size of the memory error.

text.title: Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion
text.summary: **Neural mechanism.** Spike fluctuations keep shifting the stored value after the cue has ended. The local diffusion coefficient describes the variance of those shifts after stable disturbances have relaxed. It does not by itself say that variance grows at the same rate forever: boundaries and variation of $D$ can change the long time behavior. We first keep $D$ constant, so the line and circle differ only in how the memory coordinate is bounded.

text.title: A diffusion calculation does not determine systematic drift
text.summary: **Neural mechanism.** Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original value. That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction. Both can occur, and the derivation of $D$ alone does not settle the second question.

text.title: Spike information limits memory stability
text.purpose: A neuron receiving spikes from a memory circuit has access to information about the stored value. This chapter sets a bound on estimation error under the model’s assumptions and derives the constraint that spike information places on the circuit’s memory stability.

extra_reader_text_inventory.checked: Purpose and navigation correctly frame a lower bound, not a guarantee of achieved stability. Fisher information measures local distinguishability and parameter comparisons specify fixed quantities.

text.title: Rate slopes and spike variability determine local information
text.summary: **Neural mechanism.** Suppose two nearby memory values produce almost identical rates. A short spike sample cannot reliably tell them apart. If a small change in memory instead produces a large rate change relative to spike variability, that sample is more useful. We need a quantity that measures this local distinction.

extra_reader_text_inventory.checked: Quantify whether a short spike observation can distinguish nearby memory values. The local unbiased regularity and positive-rate assumptions matter; priors or other loss functions change the question.

text.title: Spike information sets a lower bound on memory diffusion
text.summary: **Neural mechanism.** The network has no access to its exact firing rates as noiseless numbers. Its recurrent input is built from the same random spikes that an external observer sees. The lower bound on diffusion follows directly by comparing the state sensitivity of the network with the spike information.

extra_reader_text_inventory.checked: Find the unavoidable diffusion associated with internally available spike information. Positive rates, nonzero information and invertible multidimensional J are required; singular J is not inverted.

text.title: Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed

Otherwise an apparent benefit of a parameter change may come from changing another property at the same time. The comparisons below control how added neurons, altered firing rates, or slower synaptic decay affect the tuning curves and recurrent input.

text.title: Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed
text.purpose: Reading spikes from a memory circuit takes time, during which its stored value can keep changing. This chapter calculates how much longer observation can help recover the value present at a recall cue, and explains why it cannot recover every earlier random displacement.

extra_reader_text_inventory.checked: Purpose and navigation correctly separate the original value from the cue state, state the future-only observation problem, and compare equal weights, ideal inference and limited access. Exactness is confined to the Gaussian readout model.

text.title: Storage loss and readout error add under specific assumptions
text.summary: **Neural question and model.** At time $T$, a recall cue arrives. The observer now wants the original value $\Theta$, but only has access to future spikes. The network has already diffused during storage. Even perfect knowledge of the state $\theta(T)$ cannot recover its particular earlier random displacements.

extra_reader_text_inventory.checked: Separate storage error from inference error about the cue state. Storage variance2DT adds to an x-independent readout variance only with the stated unbiasedness, independence and translation assumptions.

text.title: Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long
text.summary: **Neural question and model.** A decoder designed for a stationary state averages its observations with equal weight. That reduces independent observation noise, but late observations reflect a state that has moved further from $x$.

extra_reader_text_inventory.checked: Show why equal-weight averaging eventually confuses later diffusion with better observation. This conclusion concerns equal weights and a moving state; it does not say extra data must harm an optimal estimator.

text.title: Accounting for diffusion makes readout improve toward a limit
text.summary: **Neural question and model.** An observer that accounts for diffusion can use later observations without confusing them with direct measurements of $x$. Their value is limited by the motion separating them from $x$. This is an ideal inference rule for an observer; the readout calculation does not demonstrate a neural circuit implementing it. Its error can be derived by combining information backward from the end of the observation interval.

extra_reader_text_inventory.checked: Use future measurements optimally to infer the cue state while accounting for intervening motion. The model is a benchmark observer, not a demonstrated circuit; small-h continuum limit and positiveD,J are retained.

text.title: Limited access can make observation slower
text.summary: **Neural mechanism.** A downstream area may receive only some of the memory network's spikes. That reduces its information without reducing the fluctuations that already move the full memory network.
